titleText.es: O quizás el tobogán es como Aslan y se hace más alto conmigo (pero sin la sensación de incomodidad de llegar a la adolescencia y darse cuenta de repente de todo el rollo de Cristo).
titleText.en: Or maybe the slide is like Aslan, and gets taller as I do (except without the feeling of discomfort when I reach my teens and suddenly get the Christ stuff.)
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the joke about perspective changing with age: it imagines Aslan changing size too, then pivots to readers recognizing Aslan's Christian symbolism when they are older.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO ERA UN NIÑO, EL PATIO DE MI COLEGIO TENÍA UN TOBOGÁN REALMENTE ALTO QUE SIEMPRE ME PONÍA NERVIOSO.

applications.exampleEs: TOBOGÁN REALMENTE ALTO QUE SIEMPRE ME PONÍA NERVIOSO
applications.explanationEn: Que links tobogán to the complete added information: siempre gives the repeated setting, me identifies the affected person, ponía supplies the verb, and nervioso completes the description.
Me identifies the affected person before ponía, and nervioso names that person's resulting state.

regions.labelEs: NOS MUDAMOS, PERO EL TOBOGÁN SE GRABÓ EN MI RECUERDO CONVIRTIÉNDOSE EN UN MONSTRUO RASCACIELOS.

applications.exampleEs: EL TOBOGÁN SE GRABÓ EN MI RECUERDO
applications.explanationEn: El tobogán supplies what is fixed, se grabó presents that image as becoming etched, and en mi recuerdo names the memory where it is fixed.
Convirtiéndose carries the attached se, en introduces the result, and un monstruo rascacielos fills that result slot.

regions.labelEs: AÑOS DESPUÉS, PASABA POR MI VIEJO PUEBLO Y RECORDÉ ESE PATIO.
CONDUJE HASTA EL COLEGIO PARA VER EL TOBOGÁN QUE MI YO INTERIOR DE SEIS AÑOS CREÍA TAN GIGANTESCO.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the purpose, and ver remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

applications.exampleEs: TOBOGÁN QUE MI YO INTERIOR DE SEIS AÑOS CREÍA TAN GIGANTESCO
applications.explanationEn: Que links tobogán to all the added information: mi yo interior de seis años is the person doing the thinking, creía supplies the verb, and tan gigantesco completes what that younger self believed about the slide.
Mi replaces the article to identify whose self, while yo interior supplies the fixed noun phrase.

cards.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

example.es: La casa era pequeña.
example.en: The house was small.

cards.noteEn: Patio can mean a courtyard or yard more generally. With de mi colegio, it refers to the school's outdoor play area.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio del colegio.
example.en: The children play in the school playground.

cards.noteEn: Colegio commonly means a primary or secondary school. It does not normally mean a university-level college.

example.es: Mi colegio está cerca de casa.
example.en: My school is close to home.

cards.noteEn: Tenía is a past form of tener. It presents a state or characteristic that held at that past time without marking its beginning or end.

example.es: La casa tenía un jardín.
example.en: The house had a garden.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something makes someone feel or become a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poner, identify the affected person, and add a word describing the resulting state.
cards.noteEn: Change poner to match the time and the thing causing the change. A short word such as me, te, nos, or lo can identify the affected person and goes before a conjugated form of poner: me pone nervioso. The describing word normally matches that person: nervioso for a man or boy, nerviosa for a woman or girl.

example.es: La espera me pone nerviosa.
example.en: The wait makes me nervous.

cards.answerEn: made; used to make (someone feel a certain way)
cards.noteEn: Ponía is a past form of poner used for a repeated or background past situation. With an affected person and a describing word, poner means to cause that person to enter the stated condition.

example.es: La espera me ponía impaciente.
example.en: The wait used to make me impatient.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “we” verb that is used with nos
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Nos marks the form for a group that includes the speaker. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.es: Nos quejamos del ruido.
example.en: We complain about the noise.

cards.noteEn: Nos mudamos is the completed-past form here. Mudarse means to change where one lives; nos is the matching short word used with we.

example.es: Nos mudamos a Sevilla el año pasado.
example.en: We moved to Seville last year.

cards.promptEs: algo se graba en la memoria o el recuerdo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something becomes vividly fixed in someone's memory?
cards.answerEn: Say that the thing se graba en la memoria or se graba en el recuerdo.
cards.noteEn: Grabar literally means to record or engrave. In this expression, se plus a matching form of grabar presents an image, sound, or experience as becoming etched in memory. Change graba for the time: se grabó for a completed past event, or se grabará for a future one.

example.es: Su voz se grabó en mi memoria.
example.en: Her voice became etched in my memory.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the subject as undergoing an event without naming a doer
cards.noteEn: This use of se lets Spanish focus on what receives or undergoes the action. English may use a passive form or describe the result as happening on its own.

example.es: La imagen se grabó con claridad.
example.en: The image was recorded clearly.

cards.answerEn: became etched; became fixed (in memory, with se)
cards.noteEn: Grabar literally means to record or engrave. In se grabó en la memoria or en el recuerdo, it describes an image or experience becoming firmly fixed in someone's memory.

example.es: La escena se grabó en su memoria.
example.en: The scene became etched in her memory.

cards.noteEn: Convirtiendo is the ongoing -iendo form of convertir. The attached se makes convirtiéndose part of convertirse, and en introduces the resulting identity or form.

example.es: La nube está convirtiéndose en lluvia.
example.en: The cloud is turning into rain.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes or turns into something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of convertirse, then en, then name the result.
cards.noteEn: Convertirse is used with a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos. Change convertir to match the person, thing, and time, but keep en before the resulting identity or form: se convierte en, se convirtió en, or se está convirtiendo en.

example.es: La oruga se convierte en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces the result after convertirse
cards.noteEn: After convertirse, en links the changing person or thing to what it becomes. Keep en even though English may simply use become before a noun.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.
example.en: Water turns into ice.

cards.noteEn: Rascacielos is normally the noun for a skyscraper. Here it follows monstruo as an imaginative modifier, making the monster seem as tall as a skyscraper.

example.es: Un rascacielos domina el centro de la ciudad.
example.en: A skyscraper dominates the city center.

cards.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.es: Vivimos allí durante dos años.
example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.answerEn: was passing through; used to pass (with por)
cards.noteEn: Pasaba is a background-past form of pasar. Followed by por and a place, it describes going through or by that place.

example.es: Pasaba por el centro cuando empezó a llover.
example.en: I was passing through downtown when it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

example.es: Bajamos por el sendero.
example.en: We went down the path.

cards.answerEn: old; former (a place from one's past)
cards.noteEn: Before a place connected to someone's earlier life, viejo can mean the old or former place they remember, not necessarily a physically aged place.

example.es: Volvió a su viejo barrio.
example.en: She returned to her old neighborhood.

cards.noteEn: Recordé is a completed-past form used for a memory that came to the speaker at a particular moment.

example.es: De pronto recordé su nombre.
example.en: Suddenly I remembered her name.

cards.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.es: No reconozco ese sonido.
example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: Conduje is the completed-past form of conducir used by the speaker.

example.es: Ayer conduje hasta la costa.
example.en: Yesterday I drove to the coast.

cards.noteEn: Before a place, hasta marks the endpoint reached by movement. English often uses simply to, while as far as makes the endpoint emphasis explicit.

example.es: Caminamos hasta la estación.
example.en: We walked to the station.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.es: Estudio para aprender.
example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to the private or instinctive part of someone's self?
cards.answerEn: Use el yo interior for “the inner self”; use mi, tu, or su instead of el when saying whose.
cards.noteEn: Here yo is a noun meaning self, not the subject word I. Interior stays after yo and means inner. The first word changes to identify the owner: mi yo interior, tu yo interior, or su yo interior.

example.es: Escucha a tu yo interior.
example.en: Listen to your inner self.

cards.answerEn: self (as a noun in el yo interior)
cards.noteEn: Yo normally means I. With an article or possessive word, it can instead be a noun meaning a person's self: el yo, mi yo, or tu yo.

example.es: Su yo adulto entiende la decisión.
example.en: Her adult self understands the decision.

cards.noteEn: After yo, interior describes the private inner self rather than a physical interior space.

example.es: Busca calma interior.
example.en: Seek inner calm.

cards.answerEn: aged; no separate English word before an age
cards.noteEn: De can introduce a person's age or the numerical value of an age measure. English often turns de plus the number into “aged ...” or simply states the number without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una persona de veinte años.
example.en: They are a twenty-year-old person.

cards.noteEn: Creía is a background-past form of creer. It presents a belief or opinion that was held over a stretch of past time rather than a single completed act of believing.

example.es: De niño, creía que la Luna era pequeña.
example.en: As a child, I thought the Moon was small.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.answerEn: I knew; he, she, or formal you knew; used to know
cards.noteEn: Sabía is an imperfect past form of saber, “to know.” The imperfect presents knowledge as a state that was already true or ongoing, instead of as a single completed discovery. Context tells whether the subject is I, he, she, or formal you.

example.es: Ella sabía la respuesta.
example.en: She knew the answer.
